questions.question: Model Cards (Mitchell et al., 2019) were described using which analogy, and what key section is least adopted according to Oreamuno et al. (2023)?
options: Analogous to drug package inserts; least adopted section is 'intended use'
Analogous to nutrition labels; only 0.3% of Hugging Face model cards document 'ethical considerations'
Analogous to safety data sheets (SDS); least adopted section is 'evaluation data'
Analogous to product manuals; only 1% document 'training data'
questions.explanation: Mitchell et al. introduced model cards as nutrition labels for models. Oreamuno et al. (2023) audited Hugging Face and found only 0.3% of model cards document ethical considerations — the section most relevant for responsible deployment and most commonly skipped.

questions.question: Datasheets for Datasets (Gebru et al., 2018) uses which analogy to motivate structured dataset documentation?
options: Food ingredient lists — every component must be disclosed
Electronics datasheets — standardized structured documentation that enables engineers to make informed decisions
Scientific methods sections — reproducibility requires detailed documentation
Building permits — documentation enables safety inspection
questions.explanation: Gebru et al. drew on the electronics industry analogy: components come with datasheets that systematically document specifications, limitations, and intended uses. Datasets should have equivalent structured documentation so downstream practitioners can make informed decisions about fitness for purpose.

questions.question: Data Cards (Pushkarna et al., Google 2022) introduce three 'zoom levels.' What are they?
options: Summary, detailed, and technical
Telescopic (high-level for non-experts), periscopic (middle-level for ML practitioners), and microscopic (detailed feature-level for auditors)
Executive, engineering, and legal
Model, dataset, and deployment levels
questions.explanation: Data Cards use a boundary-object framing with three zoom levels: telescopic (high-level summary readable by non-experts), periscopic (middle-level overview for ML practitioners), and microscopic (detailed feature-level documentation for auditors). The same document serves different audiences at different levels of detail.

questions.question: Laminator (Duddu et al., 2024) addresses which specific limitation of existing model cards?
options: Model cards are too long; Laminator generates compressed summaries
Model cards contain claims without proof; Laminator enables verifiable attestations via hardware TEE or cryptographic signatures attached to evaluation results
Model cards are not machine-readable; Laminator produces structured JSON outputs
Model cards become outdated; Laminator provides version tracking
questions.explanation: Laminator addresses the trust problem with model card claims: anyone can write anything. Using hardware trusted execution environments (TEEs) or cryptographic signatures, Laminator allows a model card to carry a proof-of-claim rather than just an assertion — a verifier can check the attestation independently.

questions.question: System Cards differ from Model Cards in scope. What does a System Card additionally cover?
options: It covers only the training data in greater depth than a Model Card
It covers the end-to-end AI deployment system including the safety stack, prompt-injection protection, data-exfiltration detection, incident response, and alignment with stated values
It covers the business case and financial projections for the AI deployment
It covers hardware infrastructure and compute costs for model training
questions.explanation: System Cards (Sidhpurwala 2024; formalized in 'Blueprints of Trust' arXiv:2509.20394) extend documentation beyond the model to the entire deployed system: the safety stack, prompt-injection protections, data-exfiltration detection mechanisms, alignment with stated values, and incident response procedures.

questions.question: Liang et al. (2024) found that detailed model cards on Hugging Face correlate with higher download rates. What does this demonstrate about adoption incentives?
options: Detailed cards cause downloads to increase through algorithmic search ranking
Adoption pressure is now partly market-driven — well-documented models are more trusted and more frequently selected — not only compliance-driven
The effect is spurious: popular models receive more documentation because users contribute to them
Detailed model cards reduce liability concerns, which is the primary driver of the download correlation
questions.explanation: Liang et al. report up to 29% higher download rates for models with detailed cards. This suggests the adoption problem (only 0.3% document ethical considerations) may be self-correcting as documentation becomes a competitive differentiator. Market pressure is emerging as a complementary adoption mechanism alongside regulatory compliance.
